stem:
A cohort study compares the survival rates of patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) undergoing hemodialysis (HD) at 2 different large, for-profit dialysis centers. Patients with T2DM receiving HD treatment at both centers (n = 520) are followed for 5 years. An excerpt of the results of the study is shown below.

*Analysis adjusted for age and sex.

Researchers conclude that, compared to Center A, the quality of HD treatment at Center B is suboptimal. Based on the information given, which of the following potential flaws is most likely to invalidate this conclusion?

options.A: The follow-up time is inadequate
options.B: The results are not clinically relevant
options.C: The statistical analysis did not adjust for comorbidities
options.D: The study is significantly underpowered
options.E: There is no statistically significant difference in survival rates between the centers

explanations.A: A 5-year follow-up is adequate for conditions with relatively shorter life expectancy (such as T2DM on hemodialysis) to observe a sufficient number of outcomes.
explanations.B: The absolute difference in 5-year survival (38.6% − 29.4% = 9.2%) is clinically significant.
explanations.D: Because the study detected a statistically significant difference (p = 0.0278 < 0.05), it had sufficient statistical power.
explanations.E: The p-value of 0.0278 (< 0.05) indicates a statistically significant difference.

generalExplanation: Confounding bias occurs when extraneous variables independently related to both the exposure (dialysis center) and the outcome (5-year survival) are not controlled. Although the analysis adjusted for age and sex, it failed to adjust for comorbidities (eg, cardiovascular disease, hypertension). If Center B treats sicker patients with more comorbidities, this could lower its 5-year survival rate and distort the true difference between centers.
educationalObjective: Failing to adjust for important confounders such as comorbidities can lead to confounding bias and invalid conclusions.

stem: The rheumatology department at a local university hospital participated in a randomized, prospective, open-label, parallel-group study on the clinical effectiveness of 3 new nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) in patients with osteoarthritis (OA) of knee joint. Researchers randomized 90 patients with OA of knee joint into 3 groups of 30 patients each. Patients in Group 1 received 400 mg twice daily of NSAID 1; those in Group 2 received 8 mg twice daily of NSAID 2; and those in Group 3 received 50 mg 3 times daily of NSAID 3. The primary endpoint of the study was clinical improvement in pain, stiffness, and physical function as measured by the Western Ontario and McMaster Universities Osteoarthritis Index (WOMAC). Higher scores indicate worse pain, stiffness, and functional limitations. Which of the following statistical tests is most appropriate to compare WOMAC scores among treatment groups?

options.A: Analysis of variance
options.B: Chi-square test
options.C: Correlation analysis
options.D: Relative risk

explanations.B: Chi-square test evaluates the association between 2 categorical variables.
explanations.C: Correlation analysis describes the linear relationship between 2 quantitative variables.
explanations.D: Relative risk estimates the association between a categorical independent variable and a categorical dependent variable.
explanations.E: Two-sample t-test compares the mean of a quantitative variable between 2 groups (not 3 groups).

generalExplanation: Analysis of variance (ANOVA) compares the means of ≥3 independent groups. It requires a categorical independent variable dividing participants into ≥3 groups (NSAID 1, NSAID 2, NSAID 3) and a quantitative dependent variable (WOMAC score) for which an average is calculated.
educationalObjective: The analysis of variance (ANOVA) test compares the mean of ≥3 groups using a quantitative dependent variable and a categorical independent variable.

stem: A study is conducted to identify and estimate the prevalence of the most common conditions in nursing home residents age >75. A random sample of 10 institutional long-term care facilities is selected, and 1,225 nursing home residents age >75 are included in the study. The study results showed that the 10 most common conditions among residents were high blood pressure (58%), Alzheimer disease or other dementias (45%), heart disease (33%), arthritis (25%), osteoporosis (24%), depression (22%), diabetes (18%), chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and allied conditions (17%), stroke (12%), and cancer (10%). Which of the following is a major disadvantage of this study?

options.A: The estimates are biased due to potential loss to follow-up of residents
options.B: The results of the study may be affected by ecological fallacy
options.C: The study can only identify the conditions of interest to the researcher
options.D: The study may not be able to estimate the prevalence of rapidly fatal acute conditions

explanations.A: Cross-sectional studies do not require follow-up, so loss to follow-up does not occur.
explanations.B: Ecological fallacy applies when conclusions about individuals are drawn from group-level data; here the unit of analysis is the individual resident.
explanations.C: Cross-sectional designs can identify the most common conditions in general rather than being limited to a single preselected condition.

generalExplanation: This cross-sectional study takes a snapshot of nursing home residents at one point in time to estimate disease prevalence. A major disadvantage of cross-sectional studies is late-look (Neyman) bias: they are biased toward longer-lasting, milder conditions because rapidly fatal acute conditions are less likely to be captured in a cross-sectional snapshot.
educationalObjective: Cross-sectional studies estimate disease prevalence at a single point in time but are susceptible to late-look (Neyman) bias, missing rapidly fatal acute conditions.

stem: In recent years, more people have been diagnosed with leukemia in town A than in town B. Which of the following study designs would be best suited to determine whether the town location is related to the apparent difference in leukemia incidence in these 2 towns?

options.A: Case control
options.B: Case series
options.C: Clinical trial
options.D: Cohort

explanations.A: A case-control study selects subjects by disease status and calculates an odds ratio, but cannot directly measure disease incidence.
explanations.B: A case series describes patients already diagnosed with a condition and provides no information about incidence.
explanations.C: A clinical trial compares therapeutic interventions in patients and cannot determine natural disease incidence.
explanations.E: An ecological study compares population-level rates and exposures rather than individual-level incidence.

generalExplanation: Incidence is the number of new cases arising in an at-risk population over a specified time period. A cohort study selects disease-free subjects based on exposure status (residence in town A vs town B) and follows them over time to measure and compare leukemia incidence and calculate relative risk.
educationalObjective: A cohort study is best suited for determining disease incidence and comparing incidences between exposed and unexposed groups.

stem: A clinical trial is designed to study the effectiveness of a new treatment to lower serum triglyceride levels in adults compared to the standard treatment. The researcher determined that a total of 320 patients (160 in each treatment group) would be needed to have a power of 80% to detect a difference in mean serum triglycerides of 25 mg/dL between the groups at a 0.05 significance level. At the end of the trial, the researcher reported a power of 92%. Which of the following is the most likely explanation for these findings?

options.A: The difference in mean serum triglycerides was greater than expected.
options.B: The researcher used a smaller significance level.
options.C: The sample size was reduced due to attrition.
options.D: The study was completed in a shorter amount time than expected.
options.E: The variability of serum triglycerides was greater than expected.

explanations.B: A smaller significance level (alpha) makes the threshold more stringent and decreases statistical power.
explanations.C: A smaller sample size due to attrition decreases statistical power.
explanations.D: The time required to complete a study does not directly affect statistical power.
explanations.E: Greater variability (standard deviation) in the outcome makes differences harder to detect and decreases power.

generalExplanation: Statistical power is the probability of rejecting a false null hypothesis (detecting a true difference). Power increases with larger sample size, smaller outcome variability, larger effect size (difference between groups), and a higher significance level (alpha). Because power increased from 80% to 92%, the observed difference in mean serum triglycerides (effect size) was likely greater than expected.
educationalObjective: Statistical power increases with larger sample size, smaller outcome variability, larger effect size, and higher significance level (alpha).

stem: A cohort study was conducted to assess the relationship between a high-fat diet and colorectal adenocarcinoma. The study concluded that no association exists between the exposure and the outcome after controlling for known risk factors (age, fiber consumption, and family history of cancer) as the relative risk was 1.15 with a p value of 0.25. The investigators also reported that 40% of the subjects in the high-fat group and 36% of the subjects in the low-fat group were lost to follow-up by the end of the study and were not included in the final analysis. According to this information, which of the following biases is most likely to be present?

options.A: Observer bias
options.B: Recall bias
options.C: Reporting bias
options.D: Selection bias

explanations.A: Observer bias occurs when observers misclassify data due to preconceived expectations.
explanations.B: Recall bias occurs in retrospective studies when cases are more likely than controls to recall prior exposures.
explanations.C: Reporting bias occurs when subjects under- or over-report exposures due to social stigma.
explanations.E: Surveillance bias occurs when the exposed group undergoes increased monitoring relative to the unexposed group.

generalExplanation: Substantial loss to follow-up in prospective cohort studies (here 40% in the high-fat group and 36% in the low-fat group) introduces attrition bias, a subtype of selection bias. If participants drop out for reasons related to the exposure or outcome, the remaining groups differ systematically and the estimated association may be distorted.
educationalObjective: Loss to follow-up in prospective studies creates potential for attrition bias, a subtype of selection bias.

stem:
A prospective cohort study is conducted to assess the relationship between elevated C-reactive protein level (exposure) and the development of acute coronary syndrome (disease). A sample of 100 adults age >45 is categorized according to their C-reactive protein (CRP) levels. After a 5-year follow-up period, the following data were obtained:

What is the 5-year risk of getting acute coronary syndrome in subjects with elevated CRP levels?

explanations.B: 30/100 = 0.3 is the 5-year risk of developing ACS across all study subjects.
explanations.C: 20/80 = 0.25 is the 5-year risk of developing ACS in subjects with normal CRP levels.
explanations.D: 20/100 = 0.2 is the prevalence of elevated CRP levels in the entire cohort.
explanations.E: 10/70 ≈ 0.14 is the prevalence of elevated CRP levels among nondiseased subjects.

generalExplanation: Risk (cumulative incidence) in the exposed group is the number of exposed subjects who develop the disease divided by the total number of exposed subjects at risk. Here, 10 of 20 subjects with elevated CRP developed acute coronary syndrome: 10 / 20 = 0.5 (50%).
educationalObjective: Risk in an exposed group equals the number of exposed individuals who develop the disease divided by the total number of exposed individuals.

stem: A 40-year-old woman presents to the office with several months history of atypical chest pain. Her family history is positive for hypertension and type II diabetes mellitus. Her past medical history is insignificant. An ECG stress test is performed to evaluate the possibility of coronary heart disease. This test has 85% sensitivity and 80% specificity. In the low-risk group, its positive predictive value is 25%, and negative predictive value is 96%. If the test is negative, what is the probability that the patient has coronary heart disease?

explanations.A: 25% is the positive predictive value (probability of disease given a positive test).
explanations.B: 20% (1 − specificity) is the false-positive rate.

generalExplanation: Negative predictive value (NPV) is the probability of not having the disease given a negative test result (here 96%). Therefore, if the test is negative, the probability of having coronary heart disease is 1 − NPV = 100% − 96% = 4%.
educationalObjective: If a test result is negative, the probability of having the disease is 1 − negative predictive value.

stem: A case-control study was conducted to evaluate the association between alcohol consumption and cancer of the oral cavity. The crude analysis showed a strong association between the exposure and outcome: odds ratio = 4.5, 95% confidence interval 3.4-5.6. Smoking was considered as a potential confounder of the association. Which of the following properties of smoking is necessary in order for it to be considered as a confounder?

options.A: It should not be related to cancer of the oral cavity
options.B: It should be highly prevalent in the population
options.C: It should be related to alcohol consumption
options.D: It should be observed only in alcohol consumers
options.E: It should be evenly distributed among alcohol consumers and nonconsumers

explanations.A: If smoking is not related to oral cavity cancer, it cannot be a confounder.
explanations.B: High prevalence in the population is not required for a variable to be a confounder.
explanations.D: A confounder can occur in both exposed and unexposed groups, but must be unevenly distributed between them.
explanations.E: A confounder must be unevenly distributed between exposed and unexposed groups.

generalExplanation: To be a confounder, an extraneous factor must be independently associated with both the exposure (alcohol consumption) and the outcome (oral cavity cancer) without lying on the causal pathway between them. Because alcohol users are more likely to smoke and smoking independently increases oral cavity cancer risk, smoking can confound the alcohol–oral cancer relationship.
educationalObjective: A confounder is an extraneous factor linked to both the exposure and the outcome of interest.

stem: Over the course of 2 days, 25 elderly individuals came to the emergency department of an urban medical center with acute respiratory tract infection (ARTI)—mainly bronchiolitis or pneumonitis. Public health authorities investigated the outbreak and used standardized questionnaires to collect relevant clinical and sociodemographic information from the 25 individuals with ARTI and 50 elderly individuals without ARTI matched by age, sex, and county of residence. Preliminary results showed that 92% of the elderly individuals with ARTI had attended a social gathering the previous week, and 20% of the elderly individuals without ARTI had attended the same social gathering. Which of the following statements is correct about this study design?

options.A: Because individuals with and without ARTI were matched by age, sex, and county of residence, this study is a randomized controlled trial
options.B: Because it collected data on attendance at the social gathering and presence of ARTI using a standardized questionnaire, this study is a cross-sectional study
options.C: Because it compares information about attendance at the social gathering among individuals with and without ARTI, this study is a case-control study
options.D: Because it compares the incidence of disease among elderly individuals who attended the social gathering and those who did not, this study is a cohort study
options.E: Because it describes individuals with and without ARTI in terms of clinical and sociodemographic characteristics, this study is a case series

explanations.A: Randomized controlled trials assign treatments; matching is used in observational studies (such as case-control studies) to control confounding.
explanations.B: Questionnaires can be used in case-control studies as well as cross-sectional studies; here subjects were selected by disease status (ARTI vs no ARTI).
explanations.D: Cohort studies select participants by exposure status and measure incidence; here participants were selected by outcome status.
explanations.E: Case series lack a comparison group; here a control group without ARTI is included.

generalExplanation: Because participants were initially selected based on disease status—25 cases with ARTI and 50 controls without ARTI—and then retrospectively assessed for prior exposure (attendance at the social gathering), this is a case-control study.
educationalObjective: Case-control studies select participants by outcome status (cases vs controls) and compare prior exposure frequencies.

stem: A new screening test was devised to detect pancreatic cancer at early stages using a serum marker (CA19-9) of the disease. A study of this new test showed that its use prolongs the survival of patients with pancreatic cancer by several months. The researchers concluded that use of the test improves the prognosis of patients with pancreatic cancer. Which of the following is a potential problem with this conclusion?

options.A: Observer's bias
options.B: Measurement bias
options.C: Lead-time bias
options.D: Confounding

explanations.A: Observer's, measurement, and ascertainment biases involve misclassification of outcome or exposure.
explanations.B: Observer's, measurement, and ascertainment biases involve misclassification of outcome or exposure.
explanations.D: No information is given about confounders in the study.
explanations.E: Observer's, measurement, and ascertainment biases involve misclassification of outcome or exposure.

generalExplanation: Lead-time bias occurs when a screening test detects a disease earlier than it would have presented clinically, without changing the actual disease course or time of death. This creates an illusion of prolonged survival from diagnosis to death without improving true prognosis.
educationalObjective: Lead-time bias occurs when earlier detection by screening makes survival appear longer without actually improving disease prognosis.

stem:
The drug advertisement in the exhibit button applies to the next 2 items.

A 34-year-old woman diagnosed with endometriosis 2 years ago comes to the office for follow-up. She states that she sometimes struggles to maintain focus at work due to her pain. Her primary complaint is nonmenstrual pelvic pain. The patient previously underwent laparoscopy for diagnosis and is currently not interested in undergoing hysterectomy for her endometriosis. She takes progestin but is open to trying other options for symptom relief.

Item 1 of 2
Based on the data in the ad and assuming an absolute difference of 10% in clinical response between 2 groups is clinically significant, which of the following best describes the difference in nonmenstrual pelvic pain at 6 months in both Norelia groups (low and high dose) compared to placebo?

options.A: Clinically and statistically significant difference
options.B: Clinically but not statistically significant difference
options.C: Neither clinically nor statistically significant difference
options.D: Statistically but not clinically significant difference

explanations.B: Both 97.5% CIs (2%-20% and 18%-36%) exclude the null value of 0, so the differences are statistically significant.
explanations.C: Both differences (11% and 27%) exceed the 10% clinical significance threshold and have CIs excluding 0.
explanations.D: Both differences (11% and 27%) exceed the 10% threshold for clinical significance.

generalExplanation: At 6 months for nonmenstrual pelvic pain, the absolute differences from placebo are 11% (97.5% CI: 2%–20%) for low-dose Norelia and 27% (97.5% CI: 18%–36%) for high-dose Norelia. Both exceed the 10% clinical significance threshold (clinically significant) and both CIs exclude 0 (statistically significant).
educationalObjective: A difference in rates is statistically significant when its confidence interval excludes the null value of 0, and clinically significant when it meets or exceeds the prespecified clinical threshold.

stem:
Item 2 of 2
The patient starts taking 200 mg twice daily of Norelia and has limited improvement in nonmenstrual pelvic pain at 6 months. A friend of hers, who is 43 years old and has endometriosis with a primary manifestation of dysmenorrhea, tells her that she had significant improvement at 3 months after taking 200 mg twice daily of Norelia. Which of the following statements regarding these findings is most accurate?

options.A: Due to an ecological fallacy in this study, individual differences cannot be explained
options.B: Given that these patients have different symptoms, the study results cannot be generalized to them
options.C: No significant conclusion can be drawn before 6 months of therapy have elapsed in both patients
options.D: The differences mirror the differences in primary endpoint measurements seen in the study
options.E: The friend's improvement is most likely due to the placebo effect

explanations.A: The unit of analysis in this RCT is the individual, not a population group, so ecological fallacy does not apply.
explanations.B: Both women (ages 34 and 43) fall within the trial's 18–49 age range and have the studied symptoms.
explanations.C: Significant improvement in dysmenorrhea was already evident at 3 months (75.8%) and persisted at 6 months (75.3%).
explanations.E: The friend's improvement aligns with the high dysmenorrhea response rate seen in the RCT.

generalExplanation: In the trial, high-dose Norelia (200 mg twice daily) produced higher clinical response rates for dysmenorrhea (75.8% at 3 months, 75.3% at 6 months) than for nonmenstrual pelvic pain (54.5% at 3 months, 62.1% at 6 months). Thus, the two women's differing responses mirror the study's primary endpoint results.
educationalObjective: Given different disease manifestations, the same treatment may lead to significantly different clinical outcomes.

stem: A group of investigators is planning a study to evaluate the relationship between serum fibrinogen levels and the incidence of acute coronary syndrome. They assume that serum fibrinogen levels are normally distributed in the population of interest. Which of the following statements is most consistent with this assumption?

options.A: Mean is equal to median
options.B: Mean is greater than median
options.C: Mean is greater than mode
options.D: Median is greater than mean

explanations.B: Mean > median > mode occurs in a positively (right) skewed distribution.
explanations.C: Mean > median > mode occurs in a positively (right) skewed distribution.
explanations.D: Mean < median < mode occurs in a negatively (left) skewed distribution.
explanations.E: Mean < median < mode occurs in a negatively (left) skewed distribution.

generalExplanation: A normal distribution is bell-shaped and symmetric, so its measures of central tendency are equal: mean = median = mode.
educationalObjective: In a normal distribution, mean = median = mode.

stem: In clinical practice, the "CAGE" questionnaire is used to screen patients for alcohol use disorder (AUD). When a patient replies with 2 out of 4 positive responses to the "CAGE" questions, the test is considered to be positive for AUD. If this criterion is changed so that 3 out of 4 positive responses to the "CAGE" questions label the patient as having AUD, what is the effect on the sensitivity and specificity of this test?

options.A: Both sensitivity and specificity of the test will decrease
options.B: Both sensitivity and specificity of the test will increase
options.C: Sensitivity will decrease but specificity will increase
options.D: Sensitivity will increase but specificity will decrease
options.E: Both sensitivity and specificity will remain the same

explanations.A: Raising the cutoff increases specificity while decreasing sensitivity.
explanations.B: Raising the cutoff increases specificity while decreasing sensitivity.
explanations.D: Lowering the cutoff increases sensitivity while decreasing specificity.
explanations.E: Changing the cutoff alters both sensitivity and specificity.

generalExplanation: Raising the cutoff point of a test (requiring 3/4 instead of 2/4 positive responses) makes it harder to test positive. This decreases true positives and increases false negatives (decreasing sensitivity = TP / [TP + FN]), while increasing true negatives and decreasing false positives (increasing specificity = TN / [TN + FP]).
educationalObjective: Raising the cutoff point of a screening test increases specificity and decreases sensitivity.

stem:
The drug ad in the exhibit button applies to the next 2 items.

The 3-page drug ad is focused on Efrenzia, a novel anti-platelet agent for the treatment of acute coronary syndrome.

Item 1 of 2
A 58-year-old man with a history of hypertension and type 2 diabetes mellitus comes to the emergency department because of chest pain and diaphoresis. The symptoms started 2 hours ago and have a stuttering course. He has never had similar symptoms before. In the emergency department, his electrocardiogram shows horizontal ST segment depression in leads V1 to V4. He is given the appropriate medical therapy including low-dose aspirin and referred to the catheterization laboratory due to persistence of his angina. Based on the information provided in the drug ad, giving the patient Efrenzia as opposed to clopidogrel would most likely decrease the risk of developing which of the following events?

options.A: Cardiovascular death
options.B: Major bleeding
options.C: Non-fatal stroke
options.D: Recurrent myocardial infarction

explanations.A: Page 3 of the drug ad notes there was no significant difference in cardiovascular death or nonfatal stroke.
explanations.B: Major bleeding was not part of the primary composite endpoint, and overall bleeding rates were significantly higher with Efrenzia.
explanations.C: Page 3 of the drug ad notes there was no significant difference in cardiovascular death or nonfatal stroke.

generalExplanation: Efrenzia + aspirin reduced the 18-month primary composite endpoint (cardiovascular death, nonfatal MI, or nonfatal stroke) compared with clopidogrel + aspirin in both STEMI (12.4% to 9.7%) and UA/NSTEMI (10.7% to 8.9%). However, page 3 of the ad specifies that this composite reduction was driven primarily by a significant reduction in nonfatal MIs, with no significant difference in cardiovascular death or nonfatal stroke.
educationalObjective: When comparing treatment effects on a composite outcome, it is important to examine differences between the individual component endpoints.

stem:
Item 2 of 2
Based on the drug ad data, how many patients with diabetes undergoing percutaneous coronary intervention for unstable angina (UA)/non-ST segment elevation myocardial infarction (NSTEMI) need to be treated with Efrenzia to prevent 1 additional composite event as compared to clopidogrel?
generalExplanation: In the UA/NSTEMI with diabetes subgroup, composite event incidence was 16.3% with clopidogrel + aspirin vs 12.3% with Efrenzia + aspirin. ARR = 0.163 − 0.123 = 0.04 (4.0%), so NNT = 1 / 0.04 = 25.
educationalObjective: Number needed to treat (NNT) is the inverse of the absolute risk reduction (1 / ARR).

stem: An open-label randomized parallel-arm active study evaluated the safety and efficacy of a continuous infusion of potassium chloride versus an existing intermittent infusion regimen in critically ill adults with plasma potassium concentration between 2.5 mmol/L and 3.8 mmol/L. The primary outcome was the difference in mean plasma potassium concentration over time between the 2 groups. The study reported a difference in mean plasma potassium concentration over time between groups of 0.2 mmol/L. A 90% confidence interval (CI) showed that the difference was statistically significant. What would be the effect on the width and significance of the CI if the confidence level is increased to 95%?

options.A: Width of 95% CI: Narrower; Statistical significance: Significant
options.B: Width of 95% CI: Narrower; Statistical significance: Unable to determine
options.C: Width of 95% CI: Wider; Statistical significance: Significant
options.D: Width of 95% CI: Wider; Statistical significance: Unable to determine

explanations.A: A higher confidence level (95% vs 90%) always produces a wider interval.
explanations.B: A higher confidence level (95% vs 90%) always produces a wider interval.
explanations.C: Because the boundaries of the 90% CI are not given, it is unknown whether the wider 95% CI will still exclude 0.

generalExplanation: Increasing the confidence level from 90% to 95% captures more of the distribution and always makes the confidence interval wider. However, without knowing the exact limits of the 90% CI, we cannot determine whether the wider 95% CI will remain above 0 or cross the null value of 0, so statistical significance cannot be determined.
educationalObjective: A confidence interval with a higher confidence level is always wider than one with a lower confidence level for the same data; statistical significance depends on whether it excludes the null value (0).

stem:
A 68-year-old man with severe knee osteoarthritis comes to the office to discuss options for total knee arthroplasty (TKA). The patient wants to know which type of prosthesis will help him return to his active lifestyle. A recent study compared the 10-year clinical, radiologic, and survival outcomes of single-radius (SR) prostheses and multiradius (MR) posterior-stabilized prostheses in TKA. In terms of clinical outcomes, the study reported that health survey scores were all significantly improved in both groups at the final follow-up visit (p < 0.05), with no significant differences between the 2 groups (p > 0.05). The SR group had significantly less anterior knee pain and painless crepitation (p < 0.05) compared to the MR group. Radiologic results in terms of radiolucent lines and component position angle showed no differences between the groups (p > 0.05). The Kaplan-Meier survival curve estimates at 10 years are shown below.

Based on the findings of this study, which of the following conclusions is justified?

options.A: An MR prosthesis should be recommended because its use resulted in better overall survival estimates
options.B: An SR prosthesis should be recommended because it has greater 10-year postoperative survival estimates
options.C: Both prostheses had satisfactory outcomes, but the SR prosthesis should be recommended because it may be better for pain management
options.D: Either prosthesis can be recommended because there was no significant difference in outcomes between the 2 groups
options.E: Neither prosthesis should be recommended because there was no significant difference in outcomes between groups

explanations.A: The log-rank test p = 0.57 (> 0.05) shows no statistically significant difference in 10-year survival between SR and MR.
explanations.B: The log-rank test p = 0.57 (> 0.05) shows no statistically significant difference in 10-year survival between SR and MR.
explanations.D: SR had significantly less anterior knee pain and painless crepitation (p < 0.05) than MR.
explanations.E: Both prostheses significantly improved health survey scores (p < 0.05).

generalExplanation: The Kaplan-Meier curves show no significant difference in 10-year survival (log-rank p = 0.57 > 0.05), and both groups had improved health survey scores and similar radiologic outcomes. However, the SR prosthesis had significantly less anterior knee pain and painless crepitation (p < 0.05), making it preferable for pain management.
educationalObjective: Kaplan-Meier survival curves compare event-free survival over time using the log-rank test; differences are statistically significant only if p < 0.05.

stem:
Hypothesis: Providing long-chain polyunsaturated fatty acid supplementation to pregnant women decreases the risk of asthma in their children.
Methods: Randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial at a single center in Europe; 700 pregnant women (22–26 weeks gestation) randomized to LcPUFA (N = 350) vs placebo (N = 350) with 3-year follow-up of offspring.

---

The abstract shown on the left applies to the next 2 items.

A 24-year-old woman, gravida 2 para 1, comes to the office for follow-up. She has a history of asthma and recently read about new research suggesting that polyunsaturated fatty acid supplementation in pregnancy could reduce the risk of asthma in offspring.

Item 1 of 2
According to the overall results shown in the abstract, approximately how many pregnant women would need to be treated with polyunsaturated fatty acid supplementation to prevent a case of asthma among offspring?
generalExplanation: Overall asthma incidence in offspring was 24.3% with placebo vs 17.1% with LcPUFA supplementation. ARR = 24.3% − 17.1% = 7.2% (0.072), so NNT = 1 / 0.072 = 13.89 ≈ 14.
educationalObjective: Number needed to treat (NNT) is the reciprocal of the absolute risk reduction (1 / ARR).

stem:
Item 2 of 2
The table shows the risk of asthma in the 2 groups with the children stratified according to baseline maternal blood levels of long-chain polyunsaturated fatty acids (LcPUFA). The mothers were divided in tertiles based on LcPUFA levels measured at the initiation of the trial. Based on these data, which of the following conclusions is most accurate?

options.A: Children of women in the middle tertile had a 0.8% relative risk reduction in asthma with LcPUFA supplementation.
options.B: LcPUFA supplementation should be offered to women with high baseline LcPUFA levels to reduce asthma risk among their offspring.
options.C: Leukotriene inhibitor use is likely beneficial in all pregnant women as it will increase LcPUFA levels
options.D: Personalized medicine efforts geared toward women with low baseline LcPUFA levels may be beneficial in decreasing asthma risk among their offspring.
options.E: The results of the stratified data show that the association between LcPUFA supplementation and offspring asthma is not statistically significant overall.

explanations.A: 0.8% (17.9% − 17.1%) is the absolute, not relative, risk reduction; RRR is 0.8% / 17.9% ≈ 4.5%.
explanations.B: In the highest tertile, the HR 95% CI (0.56–1.66) includes 1.0, showing no statistically significant benefit.
explanations.C: The abstract provides no information about leukotriene inhibitor use.
explanations.E: Overall, LcPUFA supplementation significantly reduced offspring asthma (HR = 0.71, 95% CI: 0.53–0.95).

generalExplanation: Stratification by baseline maternal LcPUFA tertiles shows that the protective effect is statistically significant only in the lowest tertile (18.1% vs 29.8%; HR = 0.61, 95% CI: 0.38–0.97), whereas the middle and highest tertile CIs include 1.0. Targeting supplementation to women with low baseline LcPUFA levels reflects personalized (precision) medicine.
educationalObjective: Stratification can help clarify the association between two variables and identify subgroups that benefit most.

stem: A case-control study evaluated the association between chronic cerebrospinal venous insufficiency (CCSVI) and multiple sclerosis (MS). The study enrolled 150 patients with newly diagnosed MS and 210 healthy individuals (controls) matched by age and sex. Transcranial and echo color Doppler ultrasound examinations were performed on all 360 subjects. CCSVI was present in 25 (~16.67%) patients with MS and in 10 (~4.76%) health individuals. Based on these results, which of the following is closest to the odds ratio of CCSVI in patients with MS relative to controls?
generalExplanation: In MS cases, 25 had CCSVI and 125 did not (odds = 25/125 = 0.2). In controls, 10 had CCSVI and 200 did not (odds = 10/200 = 0.05). Therefore, OR = 0.2 / 0.05 = 4.0.
educationalObjective: Odds ratio (OR) = (odds of exposure in cases) / (odds of exposure in controls) = (a/c) / (b/d).

stem:
Objective: To investigate the relationship between exercise and the use of glucose-lowering medication treatment in patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus.
Methods: Randomized controlled lifestyle intervention (12 months) in 920 patients (exercise n = 610 stratified into tertiles T1 120–240, T2 241–360, T3 >360 min/week vs standard care n = 310).

---

The abstract shown on the left applies to the next 2 items.

A 49-year-old man comes to the office for a follow-up appointment. He has type 2 diabetes mellitus that was diagnosed 6 months ago. He takes metformin twice daily but says that it makes him weak and causes abdominal pain and diarrhea. The patient does not engage in regular physical activity but says he is willing to start an exercise regimen if it will help him with his diabetes.

Item 1 of 2
Based on the study results, which of the following is the best response to this patient?

options.A: An exercise regimen of >360 min/week is the only way to increase his likelihood of discontinuing glucose-lowering medication treatment at the end of 12 months
options.B: Physical activity with a volume of exercise similar to the current recommendation of 150 min/week is needed to generate significant improvement in his HbA1c level
options.C: The patient will be significantly more likely to reduce his glucose-lowering medication treatment if he is able to exercise 150 min/week for an entire year
options.D: There is a significant chance that he can lower his HbA1c level and reduce or discontinue glucose-lowering medication treatment if he exercises >240 min/week
options.E: There is currently no statistical evidence to suggest that the patient will be able to improve his diabetes if he starts an exercise regimen now

explanations.A: Even T1 (120–240 min/week) had a statistically significant RR for medication discontinuation (RR = 12.1; 95% CI: 1.2–14.9).
explanations.B: In T1 (120–240 min/week), change in HbA1c (−0.3; 95% CI: −0.9 to 0.3) was not statistically significant because the CI included 0.
explanations.C: In T1 (120–240 min/week), medication reduction (RR = 3.7; 95% CI: 0.3–9.4) was not statistically significant because the CI included 1.0.
explanations.E: Overall, exercise significantly improved HbA1c (p = 0.003), medication discontinuation (p = 0.003), and medication reduction (p = 0.007).

generalExplanation: In T2 (241–360 min/week) and T3 (>360 min/week), all three outcomes—medication discontinuation, medication reduction, and HbA1c lowering—had 95% CIs excluding their null values (RR = 1.0 or Diff = 0). Thus, exercising >240 min/week significantly improves all three outcomes.
educationalObjective: Confidence intervals excluding the null value (1.0 for relative risk, 0 for difference in means) indicate statistical significance.

stem:
Item 2 of 2
Which of the following is the strongest additional support for a causal relationship between exercise and discontinuation of glucose-lowering medication treatment in this randomized controlled, exercise-based lifestyle intervention study?

options.A: Bias is completely eliminated by adjusting for baseline values, age, sex, and BMI
options.B: Greater exercise volumes are significantly associated with greater likelihood of discontinuing glucose-lowering medication treatment
options.C: The exercise-based lifestyle intervention had a follow-up time of 12 months
options.D: There is a significant association between intensive lifestyle intervention and discontinuation of glucose-lowering medication treatment

explanations.A: Adjusting for measured covariates reduces confounding but cannot eliminate residual or unmeasured confounding.
explanations.C: A 12-month follow-up allows outcomes to occur but is not by itself a criterion establishing causality.
explanations.D: The dose-response gradient builds upon the overall significant association to provide stronger causal support.

generalExplanation: Showing that higher exercise volumes (from T1 to T2 to T3) produce progressively higher relative risks of discontinuing medication (RR 12.1 → 25.2 → 38.9) demonstrates a biological gradient (dose-response relationship), which strengthens support for causality.
educationalObjective: A dose-response relationship (biological gradient) provides strong additional support for a causal relationship.

stem: A study was conducted to assess the relationship between race and end-stage renal disease. Two groups of pathologists independently studied specimens from 1,000 kidney biopsies. The first group of pathologists was aware of the race of the patient from whom the biopsy came, while the second group was blinded from the patient's race. The first group reported "hypertensive nephropathy" much more frequently for Black patients than the second group. This study best demonstrates which of the following types of bias?

options.A: Confounding
options.B: Respondent bias
options.C: Recall bias
options.D: Selection bias

explanations.A: Confounding involves an extraneous variable linked to both exposure and outcome.
explanations.B: Respondent bias occurs when outcomes rely on patient self-report rather than objective biopsy.
explanations.C: Recall bias results from inaccurate patient recall of past exposures.
explanations.D: Selection bias arises from how subjects are selected or lost to follow-up.

generalExplanation: Observer bias occurs when an investigator's or clinician's judgment is influenced by knowledge of exposure status (here, knowing the patient's race led pathologists to diagnose hypertensive nephropathy more frequently). Blinding prevents this bias.
educationalObjective: Observer bias occurs when an investigator's decision is adversely affected by knowledge of the exposure status.

stem: A group of infectious disease specialists interested in the rising prevalence of multidrug-resistant tuberculosis conducts a study to determine predisposing risk factors for the condition. First, they identify 40 patients with multidrug-resistant (MDR) tuberculosis and 64 with pansensitive tuberculosis who were admitted to the hospital over the last 5 years. They then review the patients' past medical records and consider demographic characteristics, previous anti-tuberculosis treatment, HIV status, and major comorbidities as potential risk factors for MDR tuberculosis development. They then compare the frequencies of these potential risk factors between the groups. Which of the following best describes the study design being used?

options.A: Case control study
options.B: Cross-sectional study
options.C: Prospective cohort study
options.D: Randomized control trial

explanations.B: Cross-sectional studies assess exposure and outcome simultaneously at a single point in time.
explanations.C: Cohort studies begin by classifying subjects by exposure status and then assess outcome development.
explanations.D: Randomized controlled trials assign subjects to interventions.
explanations.E: Retrospective cohort studies first ascertain exposure status in past records and then determine whether the outcome occurred.

generalExplanation: The researchers first selected participants by outcome status—cases with MDR tuberculosis (40) and controls without MDR tuberculosis (64 with pansensitive TB)—and then looked backward in medical records to compare prior risk factor frequencies. This is a case-control study.
educationalObjective: Case-control studies determine outcome status first and then look backward for associated risk factors, whereas retrospective cohort studies ascertain exposure first.

stem: A study was conducted to assess the association between L-tryptophan use and the development of Eosinophilia-Myalgia Syndrome (EMS). Patients with EMS were asked about the use of products containing L-tryptophan during the last 6 months. At the same time, people without EMS were randomly selected from the same population where the patients came from, and asked about their experience with L-tryptophan containing products within the last 6 months. The study showed that the use of L-tryptophan is significantly associated with EMS. Which of the following measures of association are the investigators most likely to report?

options.A: Relative risk
options.B: Median survival
options.C: Exposure odds ratio
options.D: Relative rate

explanations.A: Relative risk and relative rate require measuring incidence in cohort studies and cannot be directly calculated in case-control studies.
explanations.B: Median survival is calculated in cohort studies or clinical trials.
explanations.D: Relative risk and relative rate require measuring incidence in cohort studies and cannot be directly calculated in case-control studies.
explanations.E: Prevalence odds ratio is calculated in cross-sectional studies.

generalExplanation: This is a case-control study comparing prior L-tryptophan exposure in patients with EMS (cases) versus individuals without EMS (controls). The primary measure of association in a case-control study is the exposure odds ratio.
educationalObjective: A case-control study compares prior exposure between cases and controls, and its main measure of association is the exposure odds ratio.
